Lemma: H6237

ENGLISH GLOSSES TO TRANSLATE:
  Terse gloss: "To tithe; in Piel, to give a tenth as worship or obligation; in Qal, to exact a tenth by royal authority"
  Readable gloss: "A denominative verb built on the root for 'ten,' used in two contrasting directions. In the Piel stem it describes the voluntary, covenantal act of giving a tenth to God -- as when Jacob vowed at Bethel, 'tithing I will tithe it to you' (Gen 28:22), and in the Deuteronomic tithe laws (Deut 14:22; 26:12). In the Qal stem, however, it shifts to the ruler's power to exact a tenth: Samuel warns Israel that the king 'will tithe your grain and your vineyards' (1 Sam 8:15, 17). Spanish 'diezmar' and German 'den Zehnten' both preserve the numeric root, reflecting the universal weight of the tenth-part concept."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "give/pay a tithe (Piel)"
    Enriched: Piel: to give or pay a tenth as an act of devotion or covenantal duty. The emphatic infinitive absolute construction in Deut 14:22 ('tithing you shall tithe') underscores the obligation's gravity. Spanish 'ciertamente diezmar' mirrors this emphatic doubling. Covers Jacob's vow (Gen 28:22), the triennial tithe (Deut 26:12), and the Levitical collectors (Neh 10:38-39).
    Existing Spanish translations: Ciertamente-diezmar, cuando-diezmen, de-diezmar, diezmar, diezmarás, diezmaré-lo, los-que-diezman
  Sense 2: "exact a tithe (Qal)"
    Enriched: Qal: to take or exact a tenth, used exclusively of a king's right to levy a tithe on his subjects' produce and flocks. Appears only in Samuel's warning speech (1 Sam 8:15, 17), where the verb's active Qal form places the king as agent -- he 'will tithe' what belongs to the people, inverting the Piel's voluntary giving into compulsory extraction.
    Existing Spanish translations: diezmará
